title: Christianity: blessed are
hookLine: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers (Matthew 5:3–9)

cards: Scroll through any feed for a minute and you'll see who the world calls blessed. The rich. The winners.
The ones on the beach with the perfect caption. Hashtag blessed. Now a hillside in Galilee.
Crowds have followed Jesus, and he goes up the mountain. He sits down, the way teachers did, and the first word out of his mouth is blessed.
Then he names who's blessed, and it's almost the opposite list: the Beatitudes, the opening of the Sermon on the Mount.

teach.h: THE POOR IN SPIRIT, THE MEEK, THE MERCIFUL.
teach.b: Matthew chapter five, in the King James words: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Then those who mourn, who will be comforted. "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth."
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." The pure in heart, who shall see God.
And today's line: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Greek word behind blessed is makarios.
It can mean happy, fortunate, well off, the word for someone whose life has turned out right. So the truly well off, Jesus says, are the grieving, the gentle, the merciful, the ones making peace.

teach.h: WHO, AND WHAT'S COMING TO THEM.
teach.b: Each line has two halves: who, and what's coming to them. Many Christians read the second halves as promises about God's kingdom, partly now and fully later.
Luke's Gospel has a shorter version, set on a level place, that says simply blessed be ye poor, and adds a set of woes.
Christian readers set Matthew's poor in spirit beside Luke's plain poor, and they differ on how much to stress each.
And notice the word in today's line: not peace-lovers, peacemakers.
Making is work. It's the person who steps into the argument at the family dinner, or sends the first message after the fight.

how: Many Christians memorize the Beatitudes, and churches read them often, especially on All Saints' Day; some use them as a daily examination of how they are living.

o: people God rewards with wealth and comfort
the truly well off: the meek, merciful, peacemakers
saints the church has officially declared holy

games.q: who's blessed, and why — tap the pairs.
p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven

s: blessed in the Beatitudes means rich and comfortable
Jesus names the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek: almost the opposite list.
the Greek word, makarios, can mean happy or well off
Jesus calls the grieving and gentle the truly well off.
Luke has a shorter version with woes added
Luke 6: blessed be ye poor, and woes for the comfortable.

games.q: your family dinner is tense after an argument. the Beatitudes praise peacemakers. what's the peacemaker's move?
o: stay quiet and wait it out.
take the first step: a softer word.
win the argument, then make peace.
games.why: Jesus says peacemakers, not peace-lovers: peace here is something someone makes.

practice: Bring to mind one small tension: a sharp text you haven't answered, a cold silence at home, two friends not speaking. Don't solve it yet.
Just picture the first peacemaking step, a softer word, a question instead of a point, an apology for your part, and breathe while you hold it.
